findings.source_passage: From cradle to grave this problem of running order through chaos, direction through space, discipline through freedom, unity through multiplicity, has always been, and must always be, the task of education… a boy's will is his life, and he dies when it is broken, as the colt dies in harness, taking a new nature in becoming tame.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The attachment to Quincy was not altogether sentimental'
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is one of the book's most famous statements of its governing thesis—education as a problem of ordering chaos—and the colt-in-harness image is widely quoted and critically essential; its complete absence removes a load-bearing interpretive keystone.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at least the 'cradle to grave / running order through chaos' sentence and the colt-in-harness image verbatim in the passage on Quincy discipline and the boy-master relationship.

findings.source_passage: smell of hot pine-woods and sweet-fern in the scorching summer noon; of new-mown hay; of ploughed earth; of box hedges; of peaches, lilacs, syringas; of stables, barns, cow-yards; of salt water and low tide on the marshes; nothing came amiss.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Boys are wild animals, rich in the treasures of sense'
findings.why_it_matters: The extended, rhythmically accumulating smell catalog is prosodically distinctive and establishes the sensory richness of Adams's summer world; the draft reduces it to three items, erasing the incantatory voice and the 'nothing came amiss' capstone.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full smell inventory verbatim, including 'of ploughed earth; of box hedges; of peaches, lilacs, syringas; of stables, barns, cow-yards' and the closing 'nothing came amiss.'

findings.source_passage: The true Bostonian always knelt in self-abasement before the majesty of English standards; far from concealing it as a weakness, he was proud of it as his strength.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'A boy who began his education in these surroundings'
findings.why_it_matters: This epigrammatic sentence is a signature statement on Boston colonial psychology that the critical tradition regularly cites; its absence removes Adams's characteristic ironic inversion from the chapter's closing cultural argument.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore verbatim in the paragraph on Boston colonial atmosphere and the eighteenth-century tone of society.

findings.source_passage: One had to pay for Revolutionary patriots; grandfathers and grandmothers; Presidents; diplomats; Queen Anne mahogany and Louis Seize chairs, as well as for Stuart portraits. Such things warp young life.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The end of this first, or ancestral and Revolutionary, chapter'
findings.why_it_matters: The 'Such things warp young life' sentence is a terse, ironic verdict on inherited prestige as a burden—a key moment in the education-as-handicap motif—and the catalog it caps is rhetorically pointed; its loss flattens the funeral passage's thematic weight.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert both sentences verbatim in the funeral/death-of-the-President passage, just before or after the description of Dr. Lunt.

findings.source_passage: the history of Florence was hardly more turbulent than that of Boston? How could he whisper the word Hartford Convention before the men who had made it? What would have been said had he suggested the chance of Secession and Civil War?
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The effect of the Quincy service was deepened by the official ceremony'
findings.why_it_matters: The Florence comparison is Adams's most arresting ironic historical analogy in this chapter, and the rhetorical triple ('Hartford Convention… Secession and Civil War') builds the political charge of the Faneuil Hall scene; all three are cut, leaving only a flat paraphrase.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Florence comparison and all three rhetorical questions verbatim in the Everett Eulogy passage.

summary: The draft drops the load-bearing 'cradle to grave / colt dies in harness' passage entirely, omits the 'true Bostonian knelt in self-abasement' epigram, erases 'Such things warp young life,' cuts the Florence irony and the Hartford Convention rhetorical triple, and flattens the signature smell-catalog to three items—five distinct failures, one of them high-severity.
